script.opening: “Hello, Priya speaking. The receptionist said the doctor wanted to talk about my blood tests. I was only having them before the statin. Is something wrong?”

facts.text: “I feel fine. A bit tired, but I’m a teacher in October.”
“Actually — yes. My skin itches at night, especially my palms and soles, for about three months. I thought it was dry skin or the HRT.”
“My eyes are gritty and dry — I use drops.”
No yellow eyes or skin noticed, urine normal colour, stools normal colour. No abdominal pain, no fever or shivers, no weight loss, appetite fine, no vomiting.

“A glass of wine at the weekend.” HRT gel and progesterone since 2023, levothyroxine for years. Turmeric capsules “for my joints — about six months”. No other supplements, no recent antibiotics, no herbal teas.
No tattoos, no transfusions, no injecting drugs. Born in Kerala, moved to the UK aged 10.

facts.topic: Family (only if asked about family history or what worries you)
facts.text: “My sister Meera died of pancreatic cancer three years ago. She was 58. It started with itching and they said her liver test was off.” (Voice breaks.)

Calm and articulate at first. When you hear “liver”, ask “Is it serious?” Disclose the itch only if asked about it directly. If asked what worries you, or if the doctor says the word “cancer”, talk about Meera. If the doctor rushes to reassure without explaining, you stay anxious (“How can you know?”). If they acknowledge your sister, explain why your situation looks different, and arrange tests quickly with clear warning signs, you settle.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her sister died of pancreatic cancer that began with itching and an abnormal liver test; she fears the same.
ice.expectations: To be told whether it is serious and whether she can still start the statin.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the panel: cholestatic pattern (ALP and GGT raised more than ALT), GGT confirming hepatic origin, normal bilirubin, albumin and platelets (preserved synthetic function)
Takes a targeted history: itch, fatigue, sicca, jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pain, fever, weight loss, alcohol, medicines and supplements (turmeric, HRT), IBD symptoms, viral risk factors
Forms a differential: primary biliary cholangitis (likely), drug or supplement-induced cholestasis, biliary obstruction (stones, stricture, malignancy), PSC, infiltrative disease
Arranges liver ultrasound within about 2 weeks and a liver aetiology screen including AMA, ANA, ASMA, immunoglobulins, hepatitis B and C, ferritin, with repeat LFTs; stops turmeric
Explains urgency correctly (well, not jaundiced: urgent outpatient work-up) and the escalation path: jaundice → suspected cancer pathway or same-day assessment; fever with RUQ pain → same day
Defers the statin decision until results with a reason, and plans review and hepatology referral if AMA-positive or the scan is abnormal
Discovers and addresses the sister’s pancreatic cancer with empathy, explaining honestly why the pattern looks different and what the scan will check
Uses plain language on the phone, checks understanding, and agrees how results will be communicated

worked.txt: “The tests that relate to the bile ducts are raised, while the liver’s main working tests — how it makes protein and clears yellow pigment — are normal. So the liver is working well, but something is irritating the bile system.”
“Have you had any itching recently — especially at night or on your palms and soles?”
“You sound worried. Is there something in particular on your mind?”

“I’m so sorry about Meera. I can’t promise anything before the scan, but your results look different from what we see when a tumour blocks the bile duct — you’re not yellow, your bilirubin is normal, and you’ve lost no weight. A common cause of this pattern is an autoimmune condition called primary biliary cholangitis, which is treatable, especially in someone with an underactive thyroid like you.”
“I’m booking an ultrasound in the next couple of weeks and some extra blood tests, including one antibody test that is usually positive in that condition. Please stop the turmeric for now.”
“If your skin or eyes go yellow, your urine goes dark or your stools pale, or you get a fever with pain under your right ribs, call us the same day.”

f.learning: Abnormal liver blood tests should be interpreted by pattern: hepatocellular (ALT/AST predominant) versus cholestatic (ALP and GGT predominant), plus synthetic function (albumin, INR, bilirubin, platelets). A raised GGT with raised ALP confirms a hepatic source of ALP. The British Society of Gastroenterology recommends a standard liver aetiology screen for abnormal LFTs, including abdominal ultrasound, hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody, autoantibodies (AMA, ANA, ASMA), immunoglobulins, ferritin and transferrin saturation. In a well, middle-aged woman with autoimmune thyroid disease, nocturnal itch and sicca symptoms, a cholestatic pattern suggests primary biliary cholangitis: diagnosis rests on raised ALP plus positive AMA; first-line treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid via hepatology. Always consider drugs and supplements (turmeric has been linked with liver injury) and biliary obstruction (ultrasound). Urgency depends on the clinical picture: painless jaundice in people aged 40 and over warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer; cholangitis features need same-day assessment. Address family experiences directly and explain why the picture differs, without false certainty.

knowledge.guideline: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests (Newsome et al., Gut 2018) · BSG/UK-PBC guidelines for the management of primary biliary cholangitis (Hirschfield et al., Gut 2018) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated April 2026) · NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification (2023)
knowledge.summary: Cholestatic LFTs with normal synthetic function in a well woman: targeted history, ultrasound and aetiology screen including AMA, stop turmeric, defer the statin, safety-net for jaundice and cholangitis, and answer the fear about her sister.

points.t: Cholestatic: ALP and GGT raised more than ALT. Hepatocellular: ALT/AST predominant. GGT confirms hepatic ALP. Normal bilirubin, albumin and platelets indicate preserved liver function.

Primary biliary cholangitis; drug or supplement induced (co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, oral oestrogens, herbal products including turmeric); biliary obstruction (gallstones, stricture, pancreatic or biliary malignancy); primary sclerosing cholangitis (IBD); infiltration (metastases, sarcoid, lymphoma); congestive hepatopathy.

Liver ultrasound; AMA, ANA, ASMA, immunoglobulins (IgM raised in PBC); hepatitis B and C; ferritin and transferrin saturation; repeat LFTs; consider coeliac serology and lipid profile. Calculate FIB-4 where relevant.

Mostly women aged 40–60; associations: autoimmune thyroid disease, Sjögren’s. Symptoms: fatigue, itch, sicca. Diagnosis: raised ALP plus AMA positive. Treatment: ursodeoxycholic acid 13–15 mg/kg/day; refer to hepatology; second-line options for inadequate response; colestyramine for itch; monitor bone density.

Jaundice aged 40 or over → suspected pancreatic cancer pathway referral. Fever, rigors and RUQ pain → same-day assessment (cholangitis). Synthetic failure (raised INR, low albumin) or encephalopathy → urgent specialist input. Well and anicteric → urgent routine work-up.

Statins are not contraindicated by mildly abnormal LFTs (caution if transaminases above 3 times the upper limit). Clarifying the diagnosis first is reasonable; in PBC, high HDL is common and cardiovascular risk may be overestimated.
Pass: correct interpretation, ultrasound and AMA. Clear pass: finds the itch and the turmeric, answers the sister’s story honestly, and sets clear escalation triggers.

model.text: Hello, is that Priya Nair? It’s Dr Brennan from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth, and are you somewhere you can talk?
Yes. Is something wrong? I was only having them before the statin.
Most of the results were fine. A couple of the liver tests were raised, so I wanted to talk it through and ask a few questions. Your liver is working well overall.
Have you noticed any itching, yellow eyes or skin, dark urine or pale stools?
Actually — itching at night, palms and soles, for three months. I thought it was dry skin. Nothing yellow.
That’s helpful. Any tummy pain, fevers, weight loss, dry eyes or mouth, or change in your bowels?
model.why: Pain, cholangitis, malignancy, sicca and IBD features

model.text: Could you tell me everything you take, including anything from a shop or health store, and how much alcohol you drink?
Levothyroxine, HRT gel and progesterone, turmeric for my joints for six months. A glass of wine at weekends.
You sound worried. Is there something in particular on your mind?
My sister Meera died of pancreatic cancer. It started with itching and a liver test.

I’m so sorry. No wonder this call frightened you. I can’t give certainty until we’ve done tests, but your results look different from what happens when a tumour blocks the bile duct — you’re not yellow, the bilirubin is normal, and you haven’t lost weight.

The pattern — raised bile-duct tests, night-time itch, dry eyes, and an underactive thyroid — often fits an autoimmune condition called primary biliary cholangitis. It’s treatable with a tablet. The turmeric could also be playing a part.
model.why: Working diagnosis and differential in plain words

model.text: So: a liver ultrasound in the next two weeks to look at the liver and bile ducts, and blood tests including an antibody test for that condition, viral hepatitis, and a repeat of these. Please stop the turmeric for now. I’d hold off the statin until we have the answers.
model.why: Ultrasound, aetiology screen, stop supplement, defer statin

model.text: The gel is unlikely to cause this, so carry on with it. If the antibody test is positive, I’ll refer you to the liver team, and there’s good treatment.

Please ring us the same day if your eyes or skin go yellow, urine darkens or stools go pale, or you get a fever with pain under your right ribs. I’ll call you when the results are back. What will you do first?
Stop the turmeric, book the bloods, wait for the scan letter — and ring if I go yellow. Thank you for listening about Meera.

social.t: A sibling’s cancer frames every abnormal result; acknowledge the loss explicitly.

legal.t: Practices should have systems to act on abnormal results promptly and document the conversation and plan.

professional.t: Ask about herbal and over-the-counter products; report suspected adverse reactions via the Yellow Card scheme.
Reassurance should be specific and conditional, not absolute, before investigations.

community.t: PBC Foundation; British Liver Trust information.

ice: Concern: pancreatic cancer like her sister

playbook.diagnosis: Cholestatic liver blood tests with preserved function; probable primary biliary cholangitis (autoimmune thyroid disease, itch, sicca), with supplement-induced injury and biliary obstruction to exclude.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The bile-duct side of the liver is irritated. The liver is working well. One likely cause is an autoimmune condition that is treatable; the scan and blood tests will tell us.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened because of Meera. The scan will look directly at the bile ducts, and I’ve told you exactly what signs would mean we act the same day.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge bereavement; agree how and when results will be shared.
sharedPlan: AMA, ANA, ASMA, immunoglobulins, hepatitis B and C, ferritin, repeat LFTs
Hepatology referral if AMA positive or scan abnormal
safetyNet: Same-day contact for jaundice, dark urine, pale stools
Same-day for fever with RUQ pain

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by vague reassurance (“probably nothing, repeat in three months”) or by alarming her without a plan.

items.fail: Treats it as “slightly raised liver tests” and repeats in three months.
items.why: An ALP over twice the upper limit with raised GGT needs an aetiology screen and imaging.
items.fix: Recognise the cholestatic pattern and investigate now.

items.fail: Never asks about supplements or itch.
items.why: Turmeric and PBC are both key; itch is a major clue.
items.fix: Ask specifically about over-the-counter products and itch.

items.why: False certainty undermines trust if results change.
items.fix: Explain why it looks different, what will be checked, and what would prompt urgent action.

wordPics.clearFail: Misreads the pattern or dismisses it; no history; starts the statin without comment; no safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Arranges some tests but misses imaging or the AMA, or the turmeric and itch; the sister’s story never heard.
wordPics.pass: Interprets the cholestatic pattern, takes a targeted history, arranges ultrasound and an aetiology screen including AMA, stops turmeric and safety-nets for jaundice and cholangitis.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus finds the itch and sicca, names PBC as a likely, treatable cause, addresses the sister’s death with honest specificity, defers the statin with reasoning, and closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Your ALP and GGT are elevated with a cholestatic picture.”
avoid.instead: “The tests linked to the bile ducts are raised, but your liver is working well.”
avoid.why: Jargon on the telephone increases anxiety.

avoid.instead: “It looks different from what we see with a blockage, and the scan will check the ducts.”

avoid.dont: “Start the statin anyway — your liver will be fine.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s get the answers first, then decide about the statin.”
avoid.why: Clarifying the diagnosis first is reasonable and safer.

ro.d: Follows “is something wrong?”, “I thought it was dry skin” (cholestatic itch) and “it started with itching”.
Idea (HRT affecting her liver); concern (pancreatic cancer like her sister); expectation (is it serious; can she start the statin).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — her sister died of pancreatic cancer that began with itching and an abnormal liver test; she fears the same — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
